title: Design review of the mobile app onboarding

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Okay, I think we're just waiting for Aarav. Oh, there he is. Aarav, can you hear us?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Yes, sorry, my last call ran over. Can you hear me?

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Loud and clear. So, design review for the onboarding. We have Rafferty Quinlan presenting, Imogen Tregarthen with the research, Saskia Brouwer for product, and Aarav Chaturvedi for the iPhone side. Rafferty, go ahead and share your screen.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: Thanks, Camille. Sharing now. Can everyone see the first frame?

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: Yes, we can see it.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: Great. Quick recap. Today the onboarding is seven screens before you can write your first note. Welcome, three feature slides, account creation, contacts permission, notifications permission. My proposal cuts it to four. A welcome screen, account creation, one screen asking what you'll use the app for, and then straight into an empty note with a small hint. No contacts and no notifications during onboarding.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: No notifications at all?

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: Not during onboarding. We ask later, when there's a reason.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Before we argue about that, Imogen, can you tell us what the research said?

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: Sure. We ran sessions with twelve people last week, all new to the app. Eight out of twelve hesitated or gave up at the contacts screen. Several said something like, why does a notes app want my contacts? And on the notifications prompt, seven people tapped don't allow without reading it. Once someone says no to that system prompt, you basically can't ask again.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: That's right. The system prompt only shows once. After that, people have to dig into their settings, and nobody does.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: So we're burning our only chance on day one.

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: Exactly, Camille.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I understand the data. But I have to be honest about the other side. Ngozi's whole retention plan for next quarter is built on reminders. Without notification permission from new users, her numbers don't work.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: But Saskia, her numbers don't work now either. Seven out of twelve said no.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Seven out of twelve in a lab, Rafferty. That's not the live funnel.

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: It wasn't a lab, it was remote, on their own phones. But you're right that twelve is small.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Sorry, Imogen, I didn't mean to dismiss it. I just know what Ngozi Eze-Barnes will say when she sees no notifications in onboarding.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: What does the live data say, Saskia? What's the acceptance rate today?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: About thirty-eight percent accept on the current flow.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: That's low.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: It is low. I'm not defending the current flow. I'm saying removing the prompt completely is a big change to make behind Ngozi's back.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: I'm not removing it, I'm moving it. Look at the next frame. You save your first note, and if it has a date in it, we show a small screen that says, want a reminder for this? Only if you tap yes do we trigger the system prompt. That's what Quillfeather does, and their acceptance rate is supposedly over sixty percent.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Supposedly.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: Okay, supposedly. Aarav, you're never going to let me quote Quillfeather again, are you?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Not without a source, no.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Imogen, did any of your participants mention Quillfeather?

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: Three did, without being asked. Two said it felt calmer. That's not proof, but it's a signal.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Okay. Aarav, how hard is Rafferty's version to build?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Most of it is easy. Removing screens is easy. The reminder screen after the first note is maybe three days. The hard part is the thing Rafferty hasn't shown yet.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: Ah. You mean guest mode.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Yes. In the second version, account creation moves after the first note. So the app has to work without an account, keep everything on the phone, and merge it when you sign up. That's two weeks at least, probably three, and it breaks in strange ways.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: And we don't have three weeks. The campaign starts at the end of next month.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: I know. That's why it's version two. I'm not asking for it now.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Good. Then for this release, account creation stays where it is. Aarav, can you still give us a proper estimate on guest mode, so we can plan it?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Yes, by Friday.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Now, the contacts screen. Does anyone want to defend it?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Honestly, no. It was there for sharing, and almost nobody shares in the first week.

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: Then it should go. That was our clearest result.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Then it goes. Saskia, back to notifications. Where do you really stand?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I like Rafferty's screen. I really do. My problem is political, not design. If Ngozi hears about it from a release note, she'll block it. If she hears it from us, with Imogen's data, I think she'll at least try it.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: Can we propose it as a test? Half the new users get the old prompt, half get the new one, for two weeks.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: That's fine technically. The feature flags are already there.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Camille, a test I can sell. Ngozi will say yes to a test.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: I agree. Rafferty, you're okay with that? Your version only reaches half the users at first.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: Fine by me, Camille, as long as we actually look at the results and don't leave the old flow running forever.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Fair. We decide at the end of the two weeks, whatever the result.

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: Can I add one thing? The screen asking what you'll use the app for. Two participants found the options confusing. Work, personal, study, other. People who use it for everything didn't know what to pick.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: Good point, Imogen. I'll let people pick several, and add a skip.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Okay, let me sum up. Four screens. Contacts permission out of onboarding. Notifications asked after the first note, tested against the current flow on half of new users for two weeks. Account creation stays first. Guest mode estimated, not built.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Yes. That's it.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Actions. Rafferty, the updated prototype with the new choice screen by Monday.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: Monday, yes.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Imogen, could you run a quick round with six new people on Rafferty's prototype before we lock the design?

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: I can do six by Thursday next week. I'll book the sessions today.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Aarav, the guest mode estimate by Friday, and the test flag ready once Rafferty's frames are final.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Got it.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: And Saskia, you'll talk to Ngozi before Thursday?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I'll try for Wednesday, with Imogen's summary. Imogen, can you send me three slides, not the whole report?

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: Three slides, I promise. Maybe four.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Three, Imogen.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: And I'll send the notes this afternoon. Anything else? Rafferty, you're still sharing your screen, by the way.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: Oh. Sorry, stopping now.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Thanks, everyone. Good review.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Thanks, Camille. Bye.
